seo.title: Karmic tail 21 10 7 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 10 7 compatibility: The World at the entry, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Chariot as the main task — read through The Snow Queen.

title: The 21-10-7 karmic tail in compatibility: the whole world, eternity and a sledge of one's own
short: In The Snow Queen there is a sentence that holds the whole 21-10-7 tail. The Queen tells Kay: "When you can find out this, you shall be your own master, and I will give you the whole world and a new pair of skates." What he has to find out is a word — "Eternity". The whole world is The World, an endless circle is The Wheel of Fortune, "your own master" is The Chariot. In compatibility, the 21-10-7 tail describes a couple who enter the union wanting a whole world for two, live through it in circles, like the seasons, and learn the main thing: to choose a shared road and travel it in their own sledges, not tied to someone else's.

sections.h2: The riddle of the 21-10-7 tail: the Snow Queen's three gifts
paragraphs: The seventh story of the tale. Kay sits in an empty hall of the ice palace, blue with cold, and feels nothing: the Queen's kisses have made him numb to it. He moves flat, sharp pieces of ice about like the figures of a Chinese puzzle — Andersen calls it "the icy game of reason" (quotations from the tale follow the 1872 English translation by Mrs H. B. Paull, unless marked as ours). The ice makes whole words, but never the one word that matters — "Eternity".

For that word the Queen has promised a reward, and it has three parts. "The whole world" is The World itself, the twenty-first arcanum, the last in the row and the fullest. "Eternity" is a circle without beginning or end; Waite writes of The Wheel of Fortune as "the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe" and "the flux of human life". "Your own master" is The Chariot; for Benebell Wen the person of this card is "a master of self-control and self-assertion". The three cards of the tail stand in a single sentence. Only the order is different: for the Queen, The World is the prize at the very end, while in the tail the couple start with it.

And Kay cannot make the word. He "thought and thought until something creaked inside him" (our translation from the Danish). Then Gerda comes, her hot tears thaw the ice in his heart, he weeps, the splinter washes out of his eye, and then — Andersen makes a point of it — "it was so pleasing to see them that the pieces of ice even danced about; and when they were tired and went to lie down, they formed themselves into the letters of the word". Eternity assembled itself. Kay became his own master and got the whole world, though he never made the last move of the puzzle: "his letter of freedom stood written there in shining pieces of ice" (our translation from the Danish).

That is the riddle of the 21-10-7 tail. The three gifts — a whole world, a circle that holds, and the right to steer one's own life — can be won in two ways. One is alone, with a cold mind, as a reward. The other is together, and then the reward assembles itself, as a consequence. The tale does not say how it will turn out for a particular couple, and neither does the tail. It shows where the pieces of ice are lying.

sections.h2: How the couple's 21-10-7 tail is calculated
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not derived from its own two outer numbers. Each point of the couple is the sum of the same-named points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together.

An example is the couple 11.02.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 9-9-18, the second's is 12-19-7. Points with the same name are added: entry to entry, middle to middle, task to task.

The middle comes from the middles of the personal tails: 9 + 19. In this tail it also matches the sum of the couple's two outer numbers, 21 + 7 = 28 → 10, but that is not always so: in 50 of the 97 couple tails the middle and the sum of the outer numbers differ. This couple's centre is 9 + 5 = 14, Temperance. The couple's values are 6, The Lovers; they are not added up from the partners but recalculated from the couple's sums.

The first clue lies in the entry number itself. Twenty-one cannot come from reduction: the two personal entry points add up to 42 at most, and the digits of such numbers add up to 12 at most. So The World at a couple's entry is always an exact sum: 12 + 9, 15 + 6 or 18 + 3. One partner has a large number at this point, the other has what it takes to make twenty-one. This couple's World is put together from two parts with nothing left over — like Kay and Gerda's garden of two boxes set across the gutter.

The 21-10-7 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 41 (2.443%), 11th place among the 97 couple tails. It is formed by eight combinations of personal tails. The most common are 12-16-4 + 9-12-3 (23% of such couples), 15-20-5 + 6-8-20 (20%) and 12-19-7 + 9-9-18 (15%) — the last is exactly the couple in the example.

There are no couple tails made of the same three numbers in a different order: in a couple, 21, 10 and 7 only come this way. A personal 21-10-7 tail does exist (151 birth dates since 1900), but it is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it. A couple's tail cannot be read from the personal text, even when the numbers match.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The World: a garden of two boxes
paragraphs: The tale begins with cramped space. In a large town where "there is not room for everybody to have even a little garden", two children live in the garrets of neighbouring houses. The roofs almost meet, and between the windows runs the gutter. The parents set their boxes of roses across the gutter, the branches twine together, and, as Andersen puts it, they cluster "almost like a triumphal arch of leaves and flowers". Under this arch, on their little stools, Kay and Gerda spend the summer. The roses "seemed as if they would never leave off blooming".

This is The World at the entry to the tail: not a thing but a wish. A couple with this tail want a whole world for two — their own view of life, their own language, a space where two are never crowded. From outside, such couples often look ideal. They talked until morning on their first night and have not run out of words since. They share a philosophy, not just a household. It is easy for them to set off on the road, move to another country or live in two cities and miss each other so much that every meeting feels like the first. Waite saw in The World "joy attained in the body" and "the soul's intoxication in the earthly paradise" — a fairly exact description of the first year of such a relationship.

But The World in this position comes with a caveat, and Benebell Wen is the one who makes it. When The World lies in a spread in the position of the past, where everything begins, she writes, it suggests "the state that is predetermined or outlined" for the person — "though whether the Seeker will walk the path of manifesting that full potential is to be determined by present conditions and choices". The World at the entry is a sketch, not a title deed. The garden of two boxes is there, but the boxes stand on a gutter, and in winter no one can cross it.

The entry point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. In Andersen, that resistance has an address — the flower garden of the old woman who knew magic. There, "every flower that could be thought of for every season of the year was here in full bloom" at once, there "the sun shone and the flowers grew all the year round", and Gerda, whose hair is combed with a golden comb, forgets why she set out. The old woman is not wicked: she simply wants to keep the girl, and to do it she sinks all the roses into the ground, so that nothing reminds Gerda of the past. When Gerda finally runs out of the gate, she finds "that the summer was over, and autumn very far advanced". "Oh, how I have wasted my time!"

This is The World's shadow side in a couple. "Our world" becomes a garden of endless summer. Nothing in it may change. Friends and family are not invited. The partner's interests that do not fit the picture are mocked or forbidden, and each quietly re-educates the other to fit the common design. The days look alike, and outside it has long been autumn. The most treacherous thing about this garden is that it is beautiful.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Wheel of Fortune: one jump in summer, a peephole in winter
paragraphs: The roof garden has a feature that is easy to miss. "In summer they could be together with one jump from the window, but in winter they had to go up and down the long staircase and out through the snow before they could meet." The windows freeze, and the children warm copper pennies on the stove and hold them to the glass: "there would be very soon a little round hole through which they could peep", and an eye would appear in it — each at their own window.

This is The Wheel in the middle of the tail, the way the couple travel the path. Not in a straight line but in circles. A relationship has a summer, when the other is one jump away, and a winter, when the way to them leads down a long staircase and up again. A year when one works nights and the other days. A move after which neither has the energy to talk. Months when all the closeness there is fits into a window the size of a coin: a message at lunchtime, breakfast together on Saturdays. Lisovskaya treats cyclicity as the key to this energy in a couple: rises and crises take turns with a certain rhythm, and what has to be accepted is the change itself, rather than fought.

Benebell Wen compares The Wheel to the unit circle of school trigonometry: sine and cosine reveal "the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs, highs and lows". There is nothing broken in that picture. A slump is not a fault in the graph but its shape. The mistake is to take winter for the end of the garden.

The tale has a cold version of The Wheel too. In the Snow Queen's palace "the northern lights flared so precisely that one could count out when they were at their highest and when at their lowest" (our translation from the Danish). There are highs and lows there as well, but scheduled to the minute and lifeless. This is The Wheel's shadow side in a couple: a "silence — conflict" swing that can be predicted to the hour. Friday evening is resentment, Saturday is silence, Sunday is making up, Monday it all starts again. Both know the circle by heart, both blame it on fate or on each other. Being together is hard, but something holds them.

The Wheel of Fortune turns on Gerda's road as well. The prince and princess give her a golden coach — in a dark forest robbers seize it. The robbers nearly kill Gerda — and among them she finds the reindeer who knows the way to Lapland. Every loss leads to the next turn. And one more thing that matters for a couple: the roles on this wheel are not fixed. In the tale Kay leaves and Gerda searches, but in a couple's life winter comes to each in their own way, and the one who warmed the glass with a coin last winter may be behind the frozen window the next. Describing The Wheel in a couple, Lisovskaya recalls unions where one partner pulled the other out of a crisis. In the 21-10-7 tail this is not a division of roles but a rota.

sections.h2: Main task — The Chariot: someone else's sledge
paragraphs: "Ne v svoi sani ne sadis" — "don't sit in a sledge that isn't yours" — is a Russian proverb about not taking someone else's place; Ostrovsky gave it to a comedy as its title in 1853. In the 21-10-7 tail it can be read literally. The main point of a couple's tail, The Chariot, is read mostly through its shadow side, and Andersen draws that shadow down to the cord. The tale, by the way, carries the subtitle "in seven stories". Seven is the number of The Chariot. A coincidence, but a handy one.

In the great square the boldest boys "would often tie their sledges to country people's carts, and go with them a good way". A great white sledge appears. It drives twice round the square — The Wheel before The Chariot — and Kay quickly ties his little sledge to it. The sledge turns into the next street, the person in the white fur turns round and "nodded pleasantly to Kay, just as if they were acquainted with each other". And "whenever Kay wished to loosen his little sledge the driver nodded again, so Kay sat still". Beyond the town gate the snow comes down, and the cord can no longer be let go: "his little carriage held fast". Kay tries to say a prayer, "but he could remember nothing but the multiplication table".

Then comes a detail almost everyone passes over. The Queen seats Kay beside her, kisses him, and the first thing he remembers is not home and not Gerda: "My sledge! don't forget my sledge". The sledge is bound fast to one of the white chickens, and it flies along behind. Kay still has a sledge of his own, but now it is luggage on someone else's flight.

This is The Chariot's shadow side in a couple. One partner ties their life to the other's big goal — a career, a business, a move to wherever the job is. At first it is fun and fast; the Queen does say, "We have driven well." Each time one wants to untie, the other nods pleasantly — everything is going so well — and on they go. A few years later the town gate is far behind, and one partner's own plans have long been flying behind, tied to someone else's chicken. Among The Chariot's tasks Lisovskaya names this directly: demanding that the partner give up their own goals for someone else's. And in the shadow side she describes a couple where one adapts to the other.

The same shadow has a mirror version: both want to be the great sledge. Then the union becomes a rivalry for the lead, and every decision, from a holiday to a city, becomes an argument over whose road matters more. And there is a version where nobody steers: things get started and dropped, moves happen without a goal, passion fades fast, and a shared weariness sets in in which each drags the other down.

Why is this The Chariot's task in particular? Wen links the card to water. Upright, The Chariot is water that follows the laws of nature and "flows quickly forward, with great force"; reversed, it is "water energy being stuck or dammed up". The Snow Queen's sledge takes Kay to exactly the place where water has stopped altogether. In the middle of the palace's largest hall lies a frozen lake, "broken on its surface into a thousand forms; each piece resembled another", and the Queen "called the lake 'The Mirror of Reason,' and said that it was the best, and indeed the only one in the world". A Chariot with no direction of its own arrives at perfectly regular ice.

The tale shows other vehicles too. Leaving the prince and princess, Gerda asks for little — "a pair of boots, and a little carriage, and a horse to draw it". She is given a coach of pure gold, with the coachman, footman and outriders "all wearing golden crowns on their heads". In the dark forest the coach "lighted up the way like a torch", and the robbers see it from afar. The triumphal chariot does not get her to the goal — it draws the robbers. What gets her there is the reindeer, who was "born and brought up" in Lapland and knows the way. He, by the way, had also been tied up, "or else he would run away", and Gerda is tied onto him — the robber girl "had the forethought to tie her on". The difference is not whether someone is tied or free, but what they are tied to, and whether it knows the way.

Gerda covers the last stretch alone and barefoot: the reindeer leaves her by the bush with red berries. Before that he asks the Finland woman to give the girl "the power of twelve men". The Finland woman refuses: "I can give her no greater power than she has already, don't you see how strong that is?" In this tail, the strength that brings The Chariot to its goal is not in the harness.

At its best, Lisovskaya's Chariot looks like a team. The two are more like friends and allies, each grows outside the family as well, they make decisions together and quickly, and when they move, it is to a place they chose together. What matters is that they walk side by side, each on their own path. In the tale this is the very last frame: back home, "Kay and Gerda seated themselves each on their own chair, and held each other by the hand".

Back to the hall of ice. Kay is neither lazy nor stupid. "He told her he could do mental arithmetic, as far as fractions, and that he knew the number of square miles and the number of inhabitants in the country" — he has already counted the world. Waite says of The Chariot: "He is above all things triumph in the mind." The Snow Queen offers Kay exactly that kind of triumph: work it out in your head and you get the world. He works at it until something creaks inside him, and nothing comes.

Couples with the 21-10-7 tail have their own ice puzzles. The perfect plan that accounts for everything except what the other one wants. An agreement on who is responsible for what, drawn up so precisely that nothing alive fits into it any more. An attempt to calculate the relationship like a timetable of the northern lights. This is not stupidity. It is the best a single mind can do when the heart has frozen.

The word comes out differently. Gerda "wept hot tears, which fell on his breast, and penetrated into his heart, and thawed the lump of ice", Kay weeps himself, the splinter washes out with his tears, and the pieces of ice dance about and then lie down into the word of their own accord. In this tale eternity is not calculated. It comes when two people see each other again, and then even ice behaves as if it were alive.

And one more detail of the ending. Kay got everything he was promised: he could "be his own master, and have the whole world and a pair of new skates". But neither he nor Gerda waits for the Queen to return. They take each other by the hand and go home. The reward Kay sat over the ice for stopped mattering the moment he got it.

sections.h2: The atmosphere and values of such couples: Temperance, The Lovers and The Devil
paragraphs: The engine's figures add two more clues to the tale. The first is the centre of the couple's matrix, "The atmosphere inside the couple". In 88.1% of couples with the 21-10-7 tail it holds 14, Temperance; in the remaining 11.9%, 5, The Hierophant.

Temperance, according to Waite, bears its name because "it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures". To temper is also what a smith does to steel: heat and cold in the right measure. Hot tears on a crust of ice are Temperance at work. For a couple's atmosphere this means arguments settled by talking rather than by winning, a balance of activity and rest, the ability to wait for the right moment. In the shadow side one always gives way, the other does not notice, and it becomes unclear what the relationship is for at all. And the arithmetic gives a curious result: 14 + 7 = 21. In these 88% of couples, the atmosphere and the main task together add up exactly to the entry — Temperance and The Chariot make The World. The whole comes from measure plus direction.

Roughly one in eight such couples has The Hierophant at the centre — the card of tradition, the teacher and shared rules. Andersen has a place for it too: the grandmother who at the start tells the children about the Snow Queen, and at the end reads aloud from the Bible: "Except ye become as little children, ye shall in no wise enter into the kingdom of God." For a couple this is an atmosphere of their own rules, holidays and customs that hold the union together; in the shadow side it is lecturing and attempts to remake each other.

The second clue is "The couple's values", the spiritual purpose: what the union exists for. Here, too, couples with this tail have only two cards: 6, The Lovers, in 52.8% and 15, The Devil, in 47.2%. Waite describes both cards through one and the same pair of people. On The Lovers the two are "as if Adam and Eve when they first occupied the paradise of the earthly body". On The Devil they are the same two, "as if Adam and Eve after the Fall. Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life."

Andersen builds his tale from the same two halves. It opens with the mirror made by a hobgoblin — "he was a real demon" — and passes straight on to two children under the roses singing a hymn. The splinter of the demon's mirror strikes Kay in that very summer when the roses seemed as if they would never leave off blooming. The whole story is a journey from one picture to the other and back.

This does not mean that half of these couples have "devilish" values. The Devil in the values is about what holds people together: passion, attachment, shared ambition and money. Lisovskaya's main conclusion about this energy is that nobody belongs to anybody. The Snow Queen means to "retain her power over him", the Finland woman says, and the tale ends with a letter of freedom written in ice. The Lovers in the values are about choice and sincerity: deciding even small things together and not remaking the other to one's own standard. Wen sees in The Chariot's symbols "a continuation of certain themes that ran through Key 6: The Lovers". It can be put more simply: the sixth card is the choice, the seventh is the road after it.

sections.h2: The 21-10-7 tail on Waite's cards: the garland, the wheel and the team
paragraphs: On this site's cards the arcana have their own artwork. But the classic deck of Waite and Pamela Colman Smith holds details that finish the tale's sentence.

The World. Inside an oval garland a female figure dances with a wand in either hand, and the four living creatures stand at the corners. Waite himself calls the garland "as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things", and Wen writes that "the wreath of victory encircles her". In Andersen, between the two windows, there is "a triumphal arch of leaves and flowers". A wreath of victory and a triumphal arch of roses: the roof garden is this couple's World.

The Wheel. Waite draws it after the reconstruction of Éliphas Lévi: on one side Hermanubis rises with the wheel, on the other Typhon descends in his serpent form, and a sphinx sits at the top. In his survey of older designs Waite remarks in passing: "The wheel has seven radii." The number of the tail's main task is hidden in the spokes of its middle. And the serpent on the wheel, Wen writes, suggests "the moral choice humanity faces time and time again, not unlike the primordial choice". For couples with this tail the middle turns between the two Waite pictures from "The couple's values" — the paradise of The Lovers and the chain of The Devil. The same choice has to be made more than once.

The Chariot. The charioteer is drawn by two sphinxes — this, Waite writes, is Lévi's variation, which he adopted: "two sphinxes thus draw his chariot". "In the eighteenth century white horses were yoked to the car", and in other versions the triumphal chariot, the currus triumphalis, was drawn by other beasts as well, "as, for example, a lion and a leopard". The beasts change from deck to deck. What does not change is the question of who pulls, and where to.

And one detail that links the first and last cards of the tail. The World has two wands — in the hands of the dancing figure. The Chariot has two sphinxes — in Wen's words, "one dark and one light" — out in front, in harness. Wen calls The World "a complete reconciliation of the universe's dichotomy and duality". In The World the two are already reconciled and held lightly in the hands. In The Chariot the two are harnessed and each pulls its own way unless they are steered. A couple with the 21-10-7 tail enter the union with the first feeling — "we are one whole" — and learn the second: to drive when the team is made of two different forces.

ul: **Name the destination.** Not "onwards" and not "we'll sort something out", but where: what home, what city, what work, what kind of life a few years from now. A Chariot with no address drives in circles.

**Check whose sledge it is.** In every big decision — a move, a job, money — ask whose goal it is and what in it belongs to the other. If the answer is "nothing of mine here, but it's going so well", that is the nod of the person in the white fur.

**Know the winter route.** Agree in advance how to stay in touch when the other is not one jump away but at the end of a long staircase. The coin on the glass can be very small, but it has to be warmed.
**Don't take winter for the end of the garden.** A slump is a phase of the wheel, not a verdict on the union. Blaming fate for it is as useless as blaming each other.
**Open the windows.** A shared world stays alive as long as it can take guests: friends, family, new interests, change. A garden of endless summer is the one where the roses are sunk into the ground.
**Don't ask for the power of twelve men.** Pressure, ultimatums and "I'm stronger" do not get anyone there. What gets them there is what the Finland woman calls Gerda's own power.
**A chair for each.** Their own work, their own goals, their own time — and hands that hold each other.

paragraphs: If threats, control and fear for one's own safety have appeared in the relationship, this is no longer a matter for the tail. It calls for help from a psychologist, and in danger, a call to a local emergency number.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 21-10-7 tail
paragraphs: The tale ends where it began. Kay and Gerda go up to the grandmother's door, into "the little room, where all looked just as it used to do. The old clock was going 'tick, tick,' and the hands pointed to the time of day". The Wheel has made a full turn. "But as they passed through the door into the room, they perceived that they were both grown up." The roses on the roof peep in at the open window, and the little chairs stand where they always did.

In the strong version of the 21-10-7 tail, all three cards stay in their places but work differently. The World is not a prize for the right answer, nor a garden where time has been stopped, but a room with an open window that two people come back to from any road. The Wheel is a set of familiar seasons: both know that in winter the way to the other leads down a staircase, and they do not mistake winter for the end. The Chariot is a road chosen together, on which each has a sledge of their own and nobody flies along behind, tied to someone else's dream.

Andersen begins the tale with a promise: "when we get to the end we shall know more than we do now". And he ends it like this: "And they both sat there, grown up, yet children at heart; and it was summer,—warm, beautiful summer." That is the eternity Kay could not put together: not an endless circle, but a summer two people reached together.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 21, The World.** What the couple want together: a whole world for two — a shared view of life, open space, the road. The same wish turns into resistance when "our world" becomes a garden of endless summer, closed to change and to other people.

**N · Middle of the task — 10, The Wheel of Fortune.** How the couple travel the path: in circles. Closeness and distance, luck and slumps, the summer and winter of a relationship. The risk is to blame every turn on fate and wait for the wheel to carry them back up on its own.

**D · Main task — 7, The Chariot.** Read mostly through its shadow side: whose sledge is pulling the union. Aimless hurry, arguments over whose road matters more, the habit of tying one's own life to someone else's goal. The task is a shared direction in which each keeps a sledge of their own.

intro: The tail does not predict events, and it does not split the partners into Kay and Gerda. It shows what the couple are learning. And Andersen's tale turns out to be a surprisingly exact map of that lesson: it has a garden for two, the circle of the seasons and several teams in harness, of which only one knows the way.

faq.q: What does the 21-10-7 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix, the line of its tasks. At the entry stands The World: the wish for a whole world for two, a shared view and open space. In the middle is The Wheel of Fortune: the path runs in cycles, with rises and slumps. The main task is The Chariot: to choose a shared direction and not tie one's own life to someone else's goal. The tail does not predict events; it describes what the couple have to learn together.

faq.q: How is the 21-10-7 tail calculated in a couple's matrix?
faq.a: Each point of the couple's tail is the sum of the same-named points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. For partners born on 11.02.1976 and 05.07.1975 the personal tails are 9-9-18 and 12-19-7: 9 + 12 = 21, 9 + 19 = 28 → 10, 18 + 7 = 25 → 7. The middle is taken from the middles of the personal tails, not recalculated from the couple's outer numbers.

faq.q: How is the couple's 21-10-7 tail different from a personal 21-10-7 tail?
faq.a: They are different calculations with different roles for the points. A personal tail describes one person and is calculated from their date of birth. A couple's tail is formed from two matrices and describes the tasks of the union. Personal texts are not applied to a couple's tail, even when the numbers match.

faq.q: How common is the 21-10-7 tail among couples?
faq.a: It occurs in roughly one couple in 41, which is 2.443% — 11th place among the 97 couple tails. Most often it is formed from the personal tails 12-16-4 and 9-12-3, 15-20-5 and 6-8-20, or 12-19-7 and 9-9-18.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with 21, 10 and 7 in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these three numbers only occur in the order 21-10-7. The World at the entry of such a couple is always an exact sum: 12 + 9, 15 + 6 or 18 + 3.

faq.q: Is the 21-10-7 tail a bad sign for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail is read mostly through its shadow side because it describes tasks, not rewards. The Chariot as the main task does not say that the union is doomed; it says where the union has to learn: to choose a direction together and not to confuse a shared road with someone else's sledge.

faq.q: Which partner is Kay and which is Gerda?
faq.a: Neither, permanently. The tale helps to see how the tail works; it does not hand out roles. At different times either partner may freeze or warm the other, and the partners' sex decides nothing here.

report: Kay sat over the pieces of ice until something creaked inside him, and still he could not make the word "Eternity". For that word the Snow Queen had promised that he could be "his own master, and have the whole world and a pair of new skates". That one promise holds the whole 21-10-7 tail. The whole world is The World. Eternity, a circle without beginning or end, is The Wheel of Fortune. "His own master" is The Chariot; for Benebell Wen the person of this card is "a master of self-control and self-assertion".

Andersen calls Kay's occupation "the icy game of reason", and played alone it fails. The word comes out another way: Gerda's hot tears thaw the ice in Kay's heart, the splinter washes out, and "the pieces of ice even danced about; and when they were tired and went to lie down, they formed themselves into the letters of the word". **In this tale eternity is not calculated — it comes when two people see each other again.** A couple with the 21-10-7 tail has the same three gifts, and they too can be won two ways: alone, with a cold mind, or together.

report.h3: For the Queen the whole world is a prize; for this couple, the start

report: The tail's order differs from the Queen's: The World stands not at the end but at the entry. It is what the couple want together. Kay and Gerda had such a world from the start — a roof garden of two rose boxes set across the gutter between their windows, "almost like a triumphal arch of leaves and flowers". From outside, such couples often look ideal: they talked till morning on their first night, they share a philosophy, they set off on the road easily.

Wen adds a caveat about The World at the start: it is "the state that is predetermined or outlined", but whether the path is walked "is to be determined by present conditions and choices". **The World at the entry is a sketch, not a title deed.** And the same wish can turn into resistance. In Andersen it has an address — the old woman's garden, where flowers of every season bloom at once and "the sun shone and the flowers grew all the year round". There Gerda forgets why she set out, and when she runs out of the gate, "the summer was over, and autumn very far advanced". So "our world" becomes a garden of endless summer: nothing may change, friends and family are not invited, each quietly re-educates the other to fit the common design. The most treacherous thing about this garden is that it is beautiful.

report.h3: In summer one jump away; in winter, a staircase

report: The middle of the tail, The Wheel, is how the couple travel the path: in circles. "In summer they could be together with one jump from the window", but in winter it meant the long staircase down and up again. When the windows froze, the children warmed copper pennies on the stove and held them to the glass until "a little round hole" opened to peep through. A relationship has winters too: a year when one works nights and the other days, a move, months when all the closeness fits into a coin-sized window. Wen compares The Wheel to the unit circle: sine and cosine reveal "the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs". A slump is not a fault but the shape of the graph. **The mistake is to take winter for the end of the garden.**

There is a cold Wheel as well. In the Snow Queen's palace "the northern lights flared so precisely that one could count out when they were at their highest and when at their lowest". That is a couple's "silence — conflict" swing that both know by heart: Friday resentment, Saturday silence, Sunday making up, Monday all over again. And the roles on this wheel are not fixed: whoever warmed the glass with a coin last winter may be behind the frozen window the next.

report.h3: One's own sledge as luggage on someone else's flight

report: The main task, The Chariot, is read through its shadow side, and Andersen draws it down to the cord. A great white sledge drives twice round the square, and Kay ties his little sledge to it. The driver "nodded pleasantly to Kay, just as if they were acquainted with each other". Each time Kay wants to untie, another nod comes, and on he goes. Beyond the town gate "his little carriage held fast". When the Queen seats him beside her, his first thought is: "My sledge! don't forget my sledge". It is bound to one of the white chickens and flies along behind. **He still has a sledge of his own — but as luggage on someone else's flight.**

In a couple it looks like this: one partner ties their life to the other's big goal — a career, a business, a move to wherever the job is. At first it is fun and fast. Each time one wants to untie, the other nods pleasantly: everything is going so well. A few years on, one partner's own plans have long been flying behind. The shadow has a mirror version too: both want to be the great sledge, and every decision becomes an argument over whose road matters more.

For Wen, The Chariot is a water card: upright, water that "flows quickly forward, with great force"; reversed, "water energy being stuck or dammed up". The Queen's sledge brings Kay to a frozen lake she calls "The Mirror of Reason". A Chariot with no direction of its own arrives at perfectly regular ice.

report.h3: The reindeer knows the way, not the golden coach

report: Gerda asks the prince and princess for little — "a pair of boots, and a little carriage, and a horse to draw it". She gets a coach of pure gold; in the dark forest it "lighted up the way like a torch", and robbers seize it. The triumphal chariot does not reach the goal. The reindeer does: he was "born and brought up" in Lapland and knows the way. The robber girl "had the forethought to tie her on": what matters is not whether someone is tied, but whether what they are tied to knows the way. The Finland woman will not give Gerda "the power of twelve men": "I can give her no greater power than she has already".

Simple things change the script: saying out loud where the couple are going, not just "onwards"; asking in every big decision whose goal it is and what in it belongs to the other; knowing the winter route to each other in advance; keeping the windows of the shared world open. If threats, control and fear for one's safety have appeared in the relationship, this is no longer a matter for the tail: it calls for a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

The tale ends where it began: the same room, where "the old clock was going 'tick, tick,'". Only now Kay and Gerda "perceived that they were both grown up". **"Kay and Gerda seated themselves each on their own chair, and held each other by the hand"** — each with a sledge of their own, and one road.

unit.title: Your own sledges, one road

captions.M: To want a shared world, like a roof garden for two
captions.N: To travel in circles: a relationship's summer and winter
captions.D: To share one road without tying life to another's goal

unit.meaning: Your task is to choose one road for two and travel it in your own sledges, without tying your life to someone else's goal.
